summary: Defines the Session Description Protocol (SDP), a text format for describing multimedia sessions for announcement, invitation and other forms of session initiation. It tells endpoints what media to exchange and how to reach each other. It obsoletes RFC 4566 and is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: SDP is a text file that describes a multimedia session: which kinds of media take part, where to send them, and when the session runs. Another protocol, such as SIP or RTSP, carries that file to the other side, and both ends then read the same description.

subtitle: The plain-text format that tells endpoints what media a session carries, where to send it and when it runs.

tldr.problem: Participants in a call, a stream or a conference need a standard way to learn what media a session carries, where to send it and when it runs, whatever protocol delivers that information.
tldr.mechanism: SDP is a text format of single-letter lines (v=, o=, s=, c=, t=, m=, a= and others) written in a fixed order. A session-level section holds what is common to the session, and each media description names one stream with its transport address and format.
tldr.outcome: SDP is only a description format: it carries no transport of its own and does not negotiate content. RFC 8866 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4566.

today: RFC 8866 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It obsoletes RFC 4566, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. The RFC describes SDP as a description format only, and names SIP, RTSP, SAP, email and HTTP as the protocols that carry such descriptions.

sections.title: What SDP Is For
sections.content:
When initiating multimedia teleconferences, voice-over-IP calls, streaming video or other sessions, there is a requirement to convey media details, transport addresses and other session description metadata to the participants. SDP provides a standard representation for such information, irrespective of how that information is transported.

SDP is purely a format for session description. It does not incorporate a transport protocol, and it is intended to use different transport protocols as appropriate, including the Session Announcement Protocol in RFC 2974, the Session Initiation Protocol in RFC 3261, the Real-Time Streaming Protocol in RFC 7826, electronic mail using the MIME extensions of RFC 2045, and the Hypertext Transport Protocol in RFC 7230.

The format is intended to be general purpose so that it can be used in a wide range of network environments and applications. It is not intended to support negotiation of session content or media encodings, which the RFC places outside the scope of session description. This memo obsoletes RFC 4566.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a call or a video stream starts, the participants have to agree on what kind of media it carries, where to send it and when it runs. SDP is a standard way to write that down, and another protocol delivers the description to the other side.

sections.title: The Shape of a Session Description
sections.content:
An SDP description is entirely textual and is denoted by the media type application/sdp. Every line has the form <type>=<value>, where the type is exactly one case-significant character and the value is structured text whose format depends on that type. There are no whitespace separators on either side of the equals sign, although the value may start with whitespace that is part of its syntax.

A description consists of a session-level section followed by zero or more media descriptions. The session-level section starts with a v= line and continues to the first media description. Each media description starts with an m= line and continues to the next one or to the end of the description. In general, session-level values are the default for all media unless an equivalent media-level value overrides them.

Some lines in each description are required and some optional, but when present they must appear in exactly the order given in the RFC: v=, o=, s=, optional i=, u=, e= and p=, optional c=, zero or more b= lines, one or more time descriptions built from t=, r= and z= lines, an optional k= line, zero or more a= lines, and then the media descriptions. The fixed order greatly enhances error detection and allows for a simple parser.

The set of type letters is deliberately small and not extensible, so a parser MUST completely ignore or reject any description that contains a type letter it does not understand. Extension happens through the a= attribute lines instead, and a parser MUST ignore any attribute it does not understand. Field names and attribute names use only the US-ASCII subset of UTF-8, while textual fields and attribute values MAY use the full ISO 10646 character set in UTF-8. The text form was chosen to enhance portability and to enable a variety of transports, and the encoding is deliberately compact for environments where the maximum size of a description is limited.
sections.plainLanguage: A description is a list of lines, each starting with one letter and an equals sign, and the lines must come in a fixed order. A line the reader does not know is rejected; extra information travels in the a= lines, and an unknown a= line is simply skipped.

sections.title: Where the Media Goes
sections.content:
The c= line holds the information necessary to establish a network connection. A description MUST contain either at least one c= line in each media description or a single c= line at session level, and media-level lines override the session-level settings for their media. The line has three subfields: the network type, initially IN for Internet; the address type, initially IP4 or IP6; and the connection address.

For a multicast session the connection address is an IP multicast group address. For a session that is not multicast, it contains the unicast IP address of the expected data source, data relay or data sink, as determined by additional attribute fields. A session using an IP4 multicast connection address MUST also have a time to live value, and TTL values MUST be in the range 0 to 255. The TTL and the address together define the scope of the multicast packets sent in the session, although scoping traffic by TTL is deprecated and applications SHOULD use an administratively scoped address instead. IPv6 multicast does not use TTL scoping, so the TTL value MUST NOT be present for IP6 multicast, and scoped IPv6 addresses are expected to limit the scope instead.

For layered encodings, where the encoding from a single media source is split into layers that a receiver may subscribe to selectively, the line may name a base multicast address and the number of contiguous addresses allocated above it, as in c=IN IP4 233.252.0.1/127/3 for three addresses with a TTL of 127. The slash notation MUST NOT be used for IP unicast addresses, and multiple c= lines MUST NOT be specified at session level.
sections.plainLanguage: The c= line says where the media should go: the kind of network, the kind of address, and the address itself. For a multicast session it names the group address, and for a one-to-one session it names the other end.

sections.title: When the Session Runs
sections.content:
The t= line gives the start and stop time of a session as the decimal representation of time values in seconds since January 1, 1900 UTC. To convert these values to Unix time, subtract 2208988800. Because SDP uses an arbitrary length decimal representation, the value does not wrap in the year 2036, and implementations need to be prepared to handle these larger values. A stop time of zero means the session is not bounded, though it will not become active until after the start time; a start time of zero as well means the session is regarded as permanent. User interfaces SHOULD strongly discourage the creation of unbounded and permanent sessions, because they give no information about when the session will actually terminate and so make scheduling difficult.

A r= line specifies repeat times, with the repeat interval, the active duration and the offsets from the start time. All subfields are in seconds by default, and times may also be written with a unit character: d for days, h for hours, m for minutes and s for seconds. Fractional units are not allowed. Monthly and yearly repeats cannot be specified with a single repeat line, so separate time descriptions are used to list the session times explicitly.

An optional z= line is a modifier to the repeat fields it immediately follows, and it applies to no other fields. It gives the times at which a time zone adjustment happens and the offset from the base time, which is needed because different time zones change time at different times of day and some countries have no daylight saving time at all. Adjustments are always relative to the specified start time and are not cumulative. In this revision a z= line without a preceding r= line is a syntax error, one of the few backward-incompatible changes from the earlier specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The t= line says when the session starts and stops, counted in seconds since 1900. The r= line says how often it repeats, and the z= line says how clock changes affect those repeats.

sections.title: Media Descriptions
sections.content:
Each media description starts with an m= line and is terminated by the next m= line or by the end of the description. It has four subfields: the media type, the port, the transport protocol and one or more formats. This document defines the media types audio, video, text, application and message. The list is extended by other memos, and RFC 6466 defined the image media type.

The port is the transport port to which the media stream is sent. Other ports used by the media application, such as the RTCP port, MAY be derived from the base media port or given in a separate attribute. If noncontiguous ports are used, or the rule of even RTP ports and odd RTCP ports does not hold, the a=rtcp: attribute of RFC 3605 MUST be used. For hierarchically encoded streams sent to a unicast address, several ports can be given as m=<media> <port>/<number of ports> <proto> <fmt>, so that m=video 49170/2 RTP/AVP 31 means that ports 49170 and 49171 form one RTP and RTCP pair, and 49172 and 49173 the second.

The transport protocol subfield depends on the address type in the relevant c= line. The RFC defines udp, which carries the data directly in UDP with no additional framing, and the RTP profiles RTP/AVP, RTP/SAVP and RTP/SAVPF. The format subfields describe the media. For the RTP profiles they contain RTP payload type numbers, listed in order of preference, and the first acceptable format from the beginning of the list SHOULD be used. A dynamically assigned payload type needs the a=rtpmap: attribute, which maps the number to an encoding name, a clock rate and, for audio, the number of channels. The payload type number sits in a 7-bit field, so its values run from 0 to 127. The a=fmtp: attribute may carry format-specific parameters, and at most one instance of it is allowed for each format.
sections.plainLanguage: Each m= line describes one stream: what kind of media it is, which port carries it, which transport protocol is used and which formats are acceptable. When the transport is RTP, the formats are numbers, and a=rtpmap lines say what each number means.

sections.title: Attributes and How SDP Is Extended
sections.content:
Attributes are the primary means for extending SDP. A media description may contain any number of a= lines that add information about that media, and a= lines placed before the first media description convey information that applies to the session as a whole. An attribute takes one of two forms: a property attribute, written as a=<attribute-name>, whose presence states a property of the session, and a value attribute, written as a=<attribute-name>:<attribute-value>.

Attribute names MUST use the US-ASCII subset of ISO 10646/UTF-8, and attribute values are octet strings that MAY use any octet value except NUL, LF and CR. By default, attribute values are interpreted as ISO 10646 in UTF-8, and unlike other text fields they are not affected by the a=charset: attribute, because that would make comparisons against known values problematic. When an attribute is defined it can be defined as charset dependent. Attributes MUST be registered with IANA, and an attribute that is received but not understood MUST be ignored by the receiver.

Section 6 defines the attributes that ship with this specification. The cat and keywds attributes are obsolete and SHOULD be ignored. tool gives the name and version of the creating tool, ptime and maxptime give the length of media in a packet and the maximum length, and rtpmap maps payload types to encodings. Four attributes set the direction of the media: recvonly, sendrecv, sendonly and inactive. At most one of them MAY appear at session level and at most one in each media description, and when none is present at either level a=sendrecv SHOULD be assumed. The rest are orient, type, charset, sdplang, lang, framerate, quality and fmtp. The direction attributes apply to the media only, and an RTP-based system in receive-only or inactive mode MUST still send RTCP packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The a= lines carry everything that can be added without changing the format itself, and they are how other specifications extend SDP. A reader that meets an a= line it does not know must skip it and carry on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SDP is frequently used with the Session Initiation Protocol and the offer/answer model to agree on parameters for unicast sessions, and in that case the security considerations of those protocols apply. A session description cannot be trusted unless it has been obtained by an authenticated and integrity-protected transport protocol from a known and trusted source. Where it has not been, the endpoint SHOULD exercise care, because the media sessions received may not be the intended ones, the destination to which media is sent may not be the expected one, parameters of the session may be incorrect, or the media security may be compromised. It is up to the endpoint to make a sensible decision, which may include asking the user whether to accept the session.

Software that parses a session description MUST NOT be able to start other software except that which is specifically configured as appropriate software for multimedia participation. A session description arriving by session announcement, email, session invitation or a web page MUST NOT deliver the user into an interactive multimedia session unless the user has explicitly pre-authorized that action. As it is not always simple to tell whether a session is interactive, applications that are unsure should assume sessions are interactive.

Intermediary systems that intercept and rewrite session descriptions, for example to match NAT bindings, are NOT RECOMMENDED unless the description is carried in a manner that lets the intermediary establish its authenticity. SDP by itself does not include enough information for those checks, which depend on the encapsulating protocol. SDP MUST NOT be used to convey keying material, such as with the a=crypto: attribute of RFC 4568, unless the channel over which the SDP is delivered is both private and authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: A description on its own proves nothing: it can be changed by anyone in the middle. The RFC says to treat a description as untrusted unless it arrived over a protected channel from a known sender, and to ask the user before a received description can start any program.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 4566
sections.content:
The revision clarifies and refines terminology and aligns the terms used in the text with the ABNF: the terms <attribute>, <att-field> and "att-field" are now <attribute-name>, the terms <value> and <att-value> are now <attribute-value>, and "media" is now <media>. Three items are identified as obsolete: the a=cat: attribute, the a=keywds: attribute and the k= line, which MUST NOT be used and MUST be discarded if received.

The attribute section was reformatted for readability, and the syntax of attribute values is now given in ABNF. Sending RTCP with inactive media streams is now mandatory. The section on private sessions was removed, because the primary use of SDP is now the establishment of private sessions and SAP has fallen out of use. The a=lang: and a=sdplang: attributes were expanded and clarified, and the registration procedure for new attributes was changed and tightened.

The ABNF was revised for clarity and for alignment with the text, with backward compatibility maintained apart from a few exceptions. The syntax of time descriptions was revised to remove ambiguities, and a z= line without a preceding r= line is now a syntax error, which the RFC notes is incompatible with certain aberrant usage. The att-field rule was renamed attribute-name, with the old name kept as a synonym for backward compatibility with references from other RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: The new version tidies up the wording, marks three old features as obsolete, and rewrites the grammar so that the rules and the text agree. A few parser behaviours change, including one that older software may not accept.

v=0
o=jdoe 3724394400 3724394405 IN IP4 198.51.100.1
s=Call to John Smith
i=SDP Offer #1
u=http://www.jdoe.example.com/home.html
e=Jane Doe <jane@jdoe.example.com>
p=+1 617 555-6011
c=IN IP4 198.51.100.1
t=0 0
m=audio 49170 RTP/AVP 0
m=audio 49180 RTP/AVP 0
m=video 51372 RTP/AVP 99
c=IN IP6 2001:db8::2
a=rtpmap:99 h263-1998/90000

viz.caption: THE FOUR MEDIA DIRECTION ATTRIBUTES (RFC 8866 SECTION 6.7)

items.label: Receive-only
items.desc: Start the tools in receive-only mode. RTCP is still sent.

items.label: Send and receive
items.desc: Start the tools in send and receive mode; assumed when no direction attribute is present.

items.label: Send-only
items.desc: Start the tools in send-only mode; the control protocol is still received.

items.label: Inactive
items.desc: Send no media over the stream. RTCP is still sent.
